text:
How much of the frustration with AI comes from people who have never managed anyone? 🤔

For about ten years I worked exclusively as an engineer, and I genuinely thought that team managers were losers, and I could not see what they were needed for. 🙃 I thought that way because I was used to managing a computer, where everything is simple: you press the button and it does the thing.

Then my colleagues and I opened our own company, my manager shift started, and things turned out far more complicated, because a human being is not a computer. A machine is like a car with a steering wheel, two pedals and a gear selector, while every person is a separate spaceship running its own control system, and there is no pedal on a human that you press. You have to say something, sprinkle a bit of sugar somewhere, look into what motivation is, read up on their psychology, and only after that you can get people to give the result you need. 😅 Maybe.

I keep coming back to that shift now, because at a certain level of abstraction 𝗔𝗜 𝗯𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝗮 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗱'𝘀 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲.

I catch myself sitting there thinking: 𝘥𝘢𝘮𝘯, 𝘈𝘐, 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘴𝘰 𝘥𝘶𝘮𝘣, 𝘐 𝘥𝘰 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘵𝘰 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘺𝘰𝘶. 
And then it lands on me that literally three days earlier I had exactly the same thought about a person: 𝘐 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘧𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺, 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘰𝘯, 𝘩𝘰𝘸 𝘦𝘭𝘴𝘦 𝘥𝘰 𝘐 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘢𝘤𝘩 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘴𝘰 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘥𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘴?

Which makes me look differently at the disappointment in AI that shows up in my feed. 𝗠𝗮𝘆𝗯𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗮 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. It seems to come from people who have not managed anyone, who have not been through the hardening, and whose expectations of a model look a lot like the expectations a first-time manager has of their reports.

So the question I would put to anyone furious at a model this week is what they did the last time a person failed to understand them five times in a row. 🙃

And if we put a manager to steer an AI, they can't control the quality and fix problems because they lack engineering skills.

Which was exactly what they needed engineers for.

So it turns out, not only can't we remove any of them from the equation, we now need a person who can do both. Which kinda undermines the entire "specialization" thing.
